SEATTLE - The family of a 29-year-old U.S. Coast Guard rescue pilot who was shot and killed in Skyway is offering a $30,000 reward for information leading to an arrest in the case.

Lt. Connor Overstreet was killed early Sunday, August 23, near South 124th Street and South Langston Road, according to the King County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies were dispatched at about 12:40 a.m. after receiving reports of a shooting.

The Medical Examiner’s Office determined Overstreet died from a gunshot wound to his chest.

No suspects have been identified, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Connor Overstreet, who was shot and killed on Aug. 23 in Skyway.

What they're saying:

Overstreet’s sister, Shea Overstreet, described him as kind, thoughtful and someone who made time for anyone who needed him.

"Connor was really the best of us," Shea Overstreet said. "He was my best friend."

Overstreet was an active-duty Coast Guard pilot assigned to Air Station Ventura in California. He was here visiting Washington state for work and training. His sister said he loved flying, the outdoors, his family and his two dogs, Harry and Kenai.

"Connor loved the Coast Guard. He loved flying. He loved the challenge and the community and all he wanted to do was to help people," she said. "He wanted to save lives more than anything else."

His wife, Madeleine, also described him as her best friend and her "rock," saying in a statement that he had dedicated his life to saving others.

"All Connor wanted to do was save lives by flying for the Coast Guard," she said.

Connor Overstreet

Dig deeper:

Detectives with the Sheriff’s Office Major Crimes Unit have been canvassing the area and are looking for surveillance or dashcam video recorded between 12:30 and 1:15 a.m. Investigators are particularly interested in video showing people or vehicles.

The community has rallied raising money to increase the Crime Stoppers reward to $30,000 for a tip that leads to an arrest in the case.

Right now, no information is insignificant as far as we know, this was a random act of gun violence," said his sister.

Map of where King County deputies are seeking video in an August 23 homicide, and a QR code to submit evidence. (King County Sheriff's Office)

Shea Overstreet said the family hopes the reward encourages someone with information to speak up.

"We know that nothing can bring him back, but if we could spare one other family or anybody from having to endure this pain and loss and devastation, we’ll do that for Connor," she said.

She also urged whoever knows what happened to come forward.

"Please help us," she said. 

Tips can be submitted anonymously through the P3 Tips app or at https://t.co/HAJHQVJ1ot. Tipsters also can call 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Authorities say tipsters will not be asked to provide their names.

Shea Overstreet said the family is grateful for the support it has received as it grieves.

"Please just be kind to one another," she said. "That’s what Connor would have done. And give your loved ones one more hug,"

Before the strikes, the United States was running two tracks at once: talks in Oman and Geneva in February 2026, and preparations for military action. Reports from those sessions indicated movement on sanctions relief (as much as 80 percent in some accounts) and U.S. offers of imported nuclear fuel in exchange for limits on enrichment. The military threat remained unused and therefore still credible as a source of pressure, while Iran’s economy was already strained by sanctions and earlier 2025 strikes. That combination gave Washington room to demand longer restrictions or more verification without having already spent lives, munitions, and political capital. 
https://t.co/QfXdXH108F

Once the war began on 28 February 2026, those advantages evaporated. The campaign, which Trump initially described as a short “excursion,” lasted more than six months, cost more than $37 billion, produced U.S. casualties, and failed to collapse the Iranian government or eliminate its remaining highly enriched uranium stockpile. Iran responded by tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz, creating a new source of economic leverage that did not exist in the same form during the earlier talks. The June 2026 memorandum of understanding then offered Iran hundreds of billions in reconstruction funding and broad sanctions relief while leaving core nuclear questions (enrichment duration, disposition of 60-percent material, inspector access) for later negotiation; that framework quickly unraveled amid renewed fighting. 
https://t.co/EHUpFIJJ4o

By starting the war, Trump handed Iran enormous leverage. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump has so far proved unable to restore the level of shipping that existed before the war. That gives Iran more bargaining power in any negotiation, not less.

In short, the credible threat of force was a stronger negotiating tool than the actual, inconclusive use of force.

Trump has now burned through much of America’s available munitions and strategic oil reserves while failing to achieve his central objectives. Instead of demonstrating American strength, he has made U.S. military power look less effective—and his own strategy look incompetent.

(Sorry, I went a little deep on this one…but you made me think about some of the most important men in my life, who are no longer here, with me. Thank you for that…their memory should be honored daily! Hope you don’t mind the long response!) 🙏🏼🫶🏼

This was one of my father’s least favorite things to do. 

It was one of my middle brother’s least favorite things to do. 

It is one of my youngest brother’s least favorite things to do. 

My father & middle brother were GCs. (RIP, I miss them dearly & I think about them constantly). 

My youngest brother is also a GC. 

The men in my family have been in this profession pretty far back. I’m sure they’d all support you in this conclusion. They’re also the type that is the first to arrive at the job site & the last to leave. They work with their employees instead of just standing there, expecting them to “take orders,” & do all the work. 

My family is responsible for rebuilding & the renovations of much of Washington DC (going back a century). I have things from the U.S. Capitol Building & SCOTUS Buildings, like: the original “chandeliers” that were initially installed, when they installed electricity in the Capitol Building, parts of the roof…which my grandfather made into lanterns, drapes, mounted light fixtures, & a few other items. 

My dad was really cool, though. In the 90s there were a lot of buildings, in downtown DC that were rundown, & had turned into (for lack of a better word) “trap-houses.” 

They were full of nothing but homeless people smoking crack & shooting-up heroin. My father would spend time speaking to many of those who were in each of the buildings he bought to fix-up & sell. He would then always pick 1-2 of them & make them an offer. 

They’d be allowed to remain on the property throughout the remainder of the project, but they had to remain clean. If they required going through detox initially…he would take care of that. Their responsibilities would be to ensure no one entered the property at night while the project was closed down & workers were not present. They were to choose one of the available trades he offered. He & his crew would teach them…they were responsible for learning their chosen trade. They were responsible for the “security” of the job site. He had all of their personal details, there were contracts signed & he had a way with these guys. 

If they were dependable & picked up the trade he taught…he would offer them a full-time position at the end of the project. He paid them throughout this, fair wages, provided them with meals each day, & provided them with an appropriate place to sleep & bathe on property. 

My father was a Vietnam Veteran who served his country as a United States Marine. He suffered from severe PTSD (he dealt with this alone for many years). Many of those he helped…they were veterans, as well. Ultimately, he passed from duty related injuries (it’s on his death certificate), that were left untreated until 2011. He really didn’t start getting adequate care for them until 2017. Can you imagine? Your country willfully choosing to ignore what happened to you for 50 years…when you chose to serve & defend?

My youngest brother, he also has a soft spot for those who are facing hard times. He will hire them, provide them with living arrangements, & help them to get back on their feet.

text:
A stronger RMB can squeeze Chinese exporters, but the real strain starts if Beijing has to keep replacing those lost margins with cheaper state credit.

Japan’s experience after Plaza matters less for how far the yen moved than for what happened once the stronger currency worked through banks, credit and asset prices. West Germany took a large appreciation too without following Japan down the same path, while Japan moved into aggressive easing in 1986 as financial liberalization gathered pace, sending credit into land and equities and helping its banks expand overseas at extraordinary speed.

Basel I tightened the constraint a few years later. Japanese banks carried relatively thin core capital, while unrealized equity gains could count toward Tier 2 — comfortable while stocks kept rising, much less so once the market turned.

China has adjusted through the exchange rate before, and the RMB appreciation after 2005 coincided with a large decline in its external surplus, so the currency still matters. Since then, though, much more of China’s advantage has accumulated in intermediate goods, machinery and deeply integrated supply chains.

A stronger RMB can push up the dollar price of Chinese exports, but it cannot move a supplier cluster, a port, a power grid and an engineering workforce 20% farther away. Even when Chinese factories move to Vietnam, Mexico or Hungary, plenty of the machinery, components and financing can still trace back to China.

If that industrial network stays put while margins get squeezed, Beijing can cushion the hit through state banks, local governments and policy funds for far longer than most countries could. Doing that repeatedly means supporting exporters while refinancing local governments, recapitalizing banks, absorbing property losses and keeping strategic capacity alive, all through overlapping pools of public credit and balance-sheet capacity.

Capital controls buy Beijing even more time because much of the stress sits in RMB debt, giving China far more room than Korea had in 1997 and making a sudden IMF-style replay much harder. The losses do not disappear, though; property debt, LGFVs and industrial support keep feeding back into the same banks and public balance sheets.

China spent decades studying Japan after Plaza and Korea in 1997, then built a system designed to make both outcomes harder to reproduce. That changes the American game as well, because Washington does not necessarily need to break the system if repeated pressure keeps forcing Beijing to use it, burning more money, more credit and more balance-sheet capacity each time another exporter, strategic industry, local government or asset market needs support.

As that capacity gets scarcer, weaker firms are more likely to be cut loose while stronger firms, SOEs and local champions absorb assets and market share. The first phase could therefore leave Beijing with even more state control, while concentrating more of the financing burden inside the same system and forcing it to spend more to defend fewer positions.

Washington pays for the pressure too through higher import costs, supply-chain disruption and strain on allies, so this only works as an attrition strategy if Beijing is forced to spend more defending the system than the U.S. spends pressuring it.

Foreign equity, market access and financial opening would come later, if restructuring eventually leaves Beijing needing capital or concessions it would rather not offer. Korea showed how quickly those terms can change once balance sheets force action, while China built its capital controls and state banking system precisely to keep that moment from arriving on somebody else’s timetable.

China studied Japan and Korea and built the fortress accordingly, but every hit it absorbs costs Beijing more to hold the walls.

To wit:

“We have inherited this island.”

So this is a soft ‘we’ being employed here, and as to all the adepts of Critical Race Theory its use is two fold, it’s declarative in the sense that the historic people are expected to accept this declarative ‘we’ as the new baseline and it’s simultaneously transformative, the effect in the collective consciousness is an attempt to detach ownership from any ancient primordial historic lineage and reconnect it to a distributed open source all things to all people multi-node (the soft ‘we’) model situated permanently in the gestalt/present.

“Every generation inherits a country and redefines it.”

text:
Adam Bandt’s Bird-Brained Climate Theory
by @JamesMacpherson [COMMENTARY]

Climate change isn’t just a theory — it’s the Greens’ universal scapegoat.

Adam Bandt may not be leading the Greens anymore, but that doesn’t mean he’s given up lecturing the nation on the evils of coal and gas.

And he doesn’t need much of an excuse. Literally any reason will do.

So with the arrival of bird flu, naturally, Adam Bandt saw an opportunity to sermonise on fossil fuels.

“It’s really distressing. Like I bet you’re upset. I am too. Watching the spread of bird flu over recent weeks, it’s just been incredibly devastating.

“One of the things that this has really brought home is that it is time to stop already vulnerable populations under even more pressure by habitat destruction and climate change.”

Just one problem.

Bird flu is not caused by climate change.

But I get the temptation. Honestly, I do.

Climate change has become the Swiss Army knife of political explanations. Whatever the problem, simply unfold the climate-change blade and start waving it around…

Scientists have blamed climate change for bumpy Jetstar flights.

The ACT Government has blamed climate change for potholes.

And the World Health Organisation has blamed climate change for bad hair days.

So why not add birds with the Influence A virus to the list of casualties?

“Now is the time to stop bulldozing their habitat. Now is the time to stop opening new coal and gas mines pushing climate change even worse and making already vulnerable populations take that one step closer to extinction.”

If Adam Bandt is genuinely worried about bulldozing habitat, he might want to have a word with the renewable-energy industry.

Because there is an awkward little problem with the Greens’ vision of an all-electric, all-renewable utopia: wind and solar infrastructure does not simply materialise on pristine land after being delivered by a particularly eco-friendly fairy.

It requires roads, transmission infrastructure, substations, construction and, in many cases, the clearing and fragmentation of habitat.

Perhaps Bandt could explain why bulldozing bushland for renewable energy is virtuous, while bulldozing bushland for anything else is an unforgivable sin.

And then came the grand finale:

“We have a really significant opportunity right here, right now to offer the best protection to our wildlife, and that means stop habitat destruction and stop making climate change worse.”

There’s something almost touching about Bandt’s confidence that Australia possesses a giant planetary thermostat hidden somewhere underneath Parliament House.

Apparently, if Australia stops opening coal and gas mines, the world’s climate will breathe a sigh of relief, and bird flu will reconsider its travel arrangements.

The reality is rather less convenient.

Australia should absolutely protect wildlife habitat.

It should absolutely take bird flu seriously.

And it should absolutely scrutinise any development — renewable or otherwise — that threatens important habitat.

But turning a bird-virus outbreak into another advertisement for the climate agenda isn’t environmental leadership.

It is opportunism with feathers.

Bandt doesn’t appear to understand that bird flu isn’t caused by climate change, that renewable infrastructure can itself have environmental impacts, or that Australia alone cannot meaningfully control global temperatures by refusing to develop another coal or gas project.

But at least he has managed to find one thing that apparently has an easier time spreading than bird flu. And that’s a climate change talking point.

Read the full piece at https://t.co/xM7tKuOIBF

text:
Then the food started arriving.

Wild Mushroom Tartine with citrus crème fraîche, pickled onions and Espelette honey. The thing was huge. Rich, savory, crisp, a little sweet and gone almost immediately.

Next, the cup of Onion Soup Gratinée.

They offer two sizes, which is genius. Sometimes you want molten cheese and deeply caramelized onions without committing to a cereal bowl of it.

The cup was perfection in a cup.

The menu’s Scallop Risotto became Snapper Risotto for us, and holy hell.

Crisp-skinned snapper over wildly creamy, decadent risotto with pistou, brown-butter crumb and Parmesan. Probably my favorite dish of the night.

The kitchen handled the substitution without turning it into a thing. No committee meeting. No menu drama. Just done.

I went traditional with Coq au Vin: roasted Green Circle chicken, shallots, mushrooms, carrots and pomme purée in a proper dark, rich sauce.

Exactly what I wanted. Classics survive for a reason.

Then the Cauliflower Gratinée.

We ordered cauliflower under the fiction that we were making one responsible decision. It arrived creamy, cheesy and completely ridiculous.

Apparently cauliflower just needed better management.

The beverage program is where Boulon really got me.

Leilani Jacobs, Boulon’s bar manager, listened to what we were eating and pulled an off-list Gramercy Cellars Viognier from Washington State.

Crisp, fun, a little unexpected and somehow right with the tartine, onion soup, snapper risotto and even the coq au vin.

That’s a strange assignment for one white wine. It handled all of it.

Because I am me, I also noticed the 2017 Dom Pérignon and remember thinking the restaurant pricing looked surprisingly sane.

We didn’t order it. I was just auditing Champagne markups like a completely normal person.

Naturally, I photographed the vintage but not the price. After 25,000 steps, my documentation department had closed.

(2/3)

32 TEAMS.

32 FANTASY QUESTIONS.

LOS ANGELES CHARGERS: WHICH RECEIVER STAYS ON THE FIELD?

Los Angeles enters 2026 with plenty of reasons to like the offense.

The Chargers are projected for 23.8 points per game, 13th in the NFL, and their offensive line ranks ninth in the guide's 2026 aggregate ranking. Justin Herbert is entering his prime, while the return of Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt gives the offense a healthier foundation.

The bigger change is Mike McDaniel taking over as offensive coordinator.

His Miami offenses leaned heavily on motion, 21 personnel and running-back involvement. The guide expects the Chargers to follow that direction, potentially challenging for the league lead in heavy personnel usage.

That creates a very specific fantasy question:

Which wide receivers will actually stay on the field when Los Angeles uses two-receiver sets?

Ladd McConkey has the clearest answer. The guide views him as a near lock to remain on the field in heavy personnel, which could give him a significant advantage over his competition.

Quentin Johnston and Tre' Harris present a less certain situation.

Johnston offers a physical deep-threat profile but provides little as a blocker. Harris brings the opposite skill set and could earn more snaps than the market currently expects because of what McDaniel values from his receivers.

That matters because the Chargers had the league's No. 1 wide receiver target share last season at 68.7%.

The offense may continue producing plenty of receiver fantasy points, but the distribution could change significantly if McDaniel increases the use of heavier personnel.

When drafting a Charger, we should look beyond the projected passing volume and ask which players have a role that survives the formation changes.

For McConkey, that consistency is part of the appeal. For the other receivers, we're making a more specific bet about who wins the snaps that remain available.

32 TEAMS.

32 FANTASY QUESTIONS.

LAS VEGAS RAIDERS: WHO EMERGES BEHIND BOWERS?

The Raiders scored just 14.2 points per game last season, dead last in the NFL.

That makes the passing game difficult to trust at first glance. But Las Vegas changed the environment around it, bringing in Klint Kubiak and Kirk Cousins while adding Jalen Nailor to a receiver room that already included Tre Tucker and Jack Bech.

Brock Bowers is the clear centerpiece.

His 84% route participation ranked third among tight ends in 2025, but he averaged only 34.1 routes per game. The guide sees room for that number to increase in Year 3, particularly with very little added competition for targets.

That leaves us with a more interesting question than whether Bowers will be good.

Who captures the passing production behind him?

The Raiders have three receivers competing for that role. Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor are being drafted around WR64-70, while Jack Bech is essentially free in drafts.

The guide doesn't give us a definitive answer either.

Tucker and Nailor have the market's attention, but the analysis points toward Bech as an intriguing alternative because his skill set may fit what Kubiak's offense asks from its receivers. With the hierarchy behind Bowers still wide open, there are multiple paths to upside.

That matters for how we approach this offense in drafts.

We don't need to correctly predict which receiver becomes the clear No. 2 before the season starts. We need to recognize that the market is pricing several players as though the hierarchy is already settled.

In Best Ball especially, that creates an opportunity to take inexpensive shots at the same unresolved role.

When drafting a Raider, the question isn't simply whether the offense improves.

It's which players can capture the additional opportunity if it does—and whether we're paying for that outcome before the hierarchy has actually been established.

text:
What your parents never told you:

Based on a careers barrier to entry, its salary could be called 'Economical'-
Even if the pay gap is huge, an $80K/y casino dealer is = $160K surgeon, because the barrier to entry takes more time + skills.

Here are two lists of careers, starting from the lowest pay to the highest, of careers that are Economical and those that are Above Economical.

1. The Economical pay ladder, with the barriers that keeps each rung from flooding.

Around $100K - $120K: 
project managers, senior accountants, experienced nurses, mid-level engineers. 
The barrier is mostly experience and credentials — real, but supply still catches up over a decade, so pay stays near normal return.

$120K - $160K: 
specialized nurses, senior software engineers, experienced finance analysts. 
Now you’re adding scarce skills or location — tech hubs, hospital systems with limited residency pipelines.

$160K - $250K: physicians outside surgery, senior lawyers, quantitative analysts, airline captains. 
Licensing, years of training, and hard caps on supply — med school seats, bar passage rates, FAA limits.

$250K - $400K: surgeons, partners at big law firms, hedge fund managers, senior tech executives. 
The barrier is extreme — decades of training, tiny partnership slots, or performance that compounds.

>$400K: top surgeons, elite hedge fund managers, founders of successful companies. 
Here the barrier is often talent plus luck plus network effects, and the rent is huge because supply is nearly fixed.

2. Above-economical 

Meaning the barrier is so strong that supply never catches up — the rent sticks around for decades.

$100K - $120K: specialized trades in boom regions — oilfield welders in the Permian, union electricians in California. Licensing exists, but demand outruns training capacity, so wages sit above normal return.

$120K - $160K: nurse anesthetists, physician assistants in underserved areas, senior cloud architects. The training is shorter than a doctor’s, but the credential is scarce and demand keeps climbing.

$160K - $250K: radiologists, anesthesiologists, patent attorneys, senior derivatives traders. Residency slots and exam pass rates are hard caps — you can’t just train more people fast enough.

$250K - $400K: orthopedic surgeons, partners at top law firms, quant researchers at hedge funds. The barrier is decades plus tiny intake — a handful of fellowship spots, a handful of partnership offers a year.

> $400K: neurosurgeons, elite hedge fund managers, founders of scaled software companies. Here the rent is enormous because the barrier is nearly impenetrable — talent, network, and luck all compounding.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Top White House Advisor: The US Empire Is DYING And Socialism Is Coming Next! | David Friedberg

Overview

David Friedberg, a scientist, entrepreneur, and member of President Trump's science and technology advisory council, presents a stark diagnosis of America's current condition. He argues that the US is an empire in decline, facing an unaffordability crisis where 63% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck. He believes that a wave of socialism is absolutely inevitable, driven by national debt, government dependency, and wealth inequality. However, Friedberg is not a pessimist; he is a fierce advocate for individual agency, capitalism, and technological progress. He sees AI as a golden age that will expand the economy and create new opportunities, not destroy jobs. His core prescription is to fix the tax code to address inequality without seizing assets, reform government incentives to curb short-termism, and trust in the historical power of free markets and individual liberty to solve our problems.

Key Themes

- The US empire is in decline, marked by economic distress where 63% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck and costs outpace wages, a condition that historically leads to internal strife and external conflict.
- A shift toward socialism is inevitable because of compounding national debt, Federal Reserve policy, and roughly half the population relying on government employment or benefits.
- AI is a golden age and the most important subject of our time; it will not cause mass unemployment because technological revolutions have historically increased jobs and incomes by boosting productivity.
- The tax code, not capitalism, is the root of wealth inequality; capital gains compound untaxed while labor is taxed every paycheck, making a flat tax on capital the solution.
- The American Dream is not homeownership but the transition from labor to capital, moving from living on paychecks to living on asset income.
- Government expansion is a failure; services it touches, like education and housing, become more expensive, and the great lie is that the government will save you.
- Open-source AI models are a hedge against wealth concentration, offering a path for new billionaires to emerge from nowhere and challenging the dominance of big tech players.
- A policy shift toward the "Denmark model" of high taxes and social services would erode the liberty and incentives that drive American progress, a tradeoff that is likely unsolvable.

Detailed Summary

Friedberg frames the American condition as an empire in decline, pointing to Ray Dalio's "cycle of empires" theory, which tracks the rise and fall of six empires over 500 years, with the US declining and China rising. He connects this internal economic distress to foreign policy, claiming that unhappy nations go to war, while happy nations do not. The unaffordability crisis is central to this decline; with 63% of Americans having less than $500 in savings, the social fabric is strained. This economic pain, he argues, makes a wave of socialism inevitable, as a majority of Americans become reliant on government employment or support.

Friedberg’s primary enemy is not capitalism but a flawed tax policy. He explains that labor is taxed on every paycheck, while capital gains are only taxed when an asset is sold, allowing wealth to compound tax-free. This creates an inherent advantage for asset holders. His proposed fix is to tax capital at the same rate as labor, ideally at the moment of transaction. He strongly rejects a wealth tax, calling it an "asset seizure" that is antithetical to the US founding principle of private property rights and likely unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment. He cites France's failed wealth tax, which drove wealthy individuals out of the country and reduced total tax revenue, as evidence.

Friedberg elaborates on how the wealthy avoid taxes through borrowing. Banks offer loans against stock holdings at low interest rates, allowing individuals to fund large purchases without selling assets and triggering a taxable event. He frames this as a loophole that should be a taxable event. He also dismantles the "great American dream" of homeownership, calling it a "great lie" that concentrates capital in one asset and inflates prices, making homes unaffordable for younger generations while enriching existing owners. He suggests that investing in the S&P 500, which averages 10-11% annual returns, is a more effective path to building wealth.

The speaker’s core philosophy is that individual agency, not government intervention, is the solution to economic hardship. He advises young people to ask themselves, "What did you do today that someone else valued?" and to repeat that. He points to the internet as an unprecedented enabler for new income paths, from podcasting to online selling. The host pushes back, noting that government infrastructure like free schooling, healthcare, and a social safety net provided the stable foundation that enabled his own risk-taking. Friedberg acknowledges the tension, arguing that the goal is a balance between government dependency and a universal entrepreneur path, focusing on an individual's capacity to create value.

On AI, Friedberg is unwaveringly optimistic. He argues that technological revolutions have never led to net job loss, citing the shift from farming to factory work and the panic over computers in the 1960s and 1980s. He sees AI as a tool for creative leverage, enabling one person to do the work of a team. He counters the idea of a "fixed pie" economy, asserting that automation expands the economy and benefits workers over time. He predicts that AI will compress routine knowledge work, freeing up time for other value creation, and that in-person experiences will become more valuable as automation handles routine tasks.

Friedberg is critical of AI leaders who warn of existential risk, pointing to their inconsistent narratives. He cites Sam Altman's shift from calling AI the "greatest threat to humanity" in 2015 to later reassuring the public, and Elon Musk's 2014 warning about "summoning the demon." He also disputes the narrative that AI is causing job losses, using Klarna as an example. While Klarna's founder confirmed he is cutting staff due to AI, the company's revenue doubled, and it rehired for VIP services. Friedberg argues that cost savings enable companies to invest in new products, which drives hiring. The real question, he insists, is not whether to slow AI development, which is "too far too late," but where data centers and models are built—domestically or offshore.

Friedberg champions open-source AI as a tool against wealth concentration. He notes that Chinese open-source models can be as good as or better than private American models at a fraction of the cost. He dismisses concerns about Chinese models as backdoor programs, explaining that they are just "a list of numbers." He predicts that within a decade, a new billionaire will emerge from building a company on open-source AI, challenging the idea that big players like Elon Musk or Sam Altman will capture all the value.

Finally, Friedberg addresses the fear of socialism by outlining his vision for a better path. He calls for term limits for politicians and a rotation between public and private life to combat the short-termism of four-year election cycles. He argues that the choice for America is between "inequality or lack of progress," using the "golden goose" analogy to illustrate that while early adopters of technology race ahead, value eventually diffuses to everyone. He rejects the "Denmark model" of high taxes and universal services, arguing that it would erode the freedom and incentives that drive entrepreneurial risk-taking and frontier progress, like life-saving CART-T cancer therapies. He believes the answer is not to confiscate wealth from the top, but to enable the bottom 50% to build capital and achieve the transition from labor to capital themselves.
